4 years later, this is still easily the best multiplayer horror game I've ever played.

DEVOUR manages to combine a feeling of chaos and dread and mixes it masterfully with elements of strategy, encouraging you to play the game for the first time screaming your head off, jumping at every shadow. Then, for your next few attempts, you plan ahead with your buddies (or if you're masochistic, yourself) to achieve victory and banish the goat demon Azazel who has taken various forms to thwart your progress.

The game is a slow-burn experience, meaning that the more progress you achieve, the more aggressive the game will become. Better strap in, because this game will not stop throwing everything it can at you.

As someone who has played since The Inn (2021) was released, I feel a sense of pride seeing how far the developers have come since the first map was released. You can tell they're putting their heart and soul into each new map release (which are COMPLETELY FREE, BY THE WAY), and manage to outdo themselves time and time again, whether it's the music that is expertly composed by Steve Brooks, the terrifying voice acting for each monster, or the sound design of each map and monster that keeps you on your toes. 

The Azazel (the main monster) is exclusive to their respective map. Your antagonist can range from a gun-toting sheriff with an itchy trigger finger to a nasty pig-man who will be on top of you in half a second. Regardless of their quirks and strengths, one thing remains the same. They will catch you, and they will make it hurt. (Or in a lot of cases, hurt your eardrums. Those jumpscare sounds are no joke.) Every design is unique and tells a long story of the agonizing process the monster took to reach their condition.

It's no secret that I love DEVOUR, and have dedicated a lot of time to mastering each and every map in the game, DEVOUR has brought me so much joy and scares that I find myself coming back to this game more often than any other horror title.

I can't recommend this game enough.

Just give me a flamethrower ffs..

Game itself is fun as long as you don't mind some repetition. Your job is to exorcise one of your fellow friends and cult members possessed by the demon Azazel, because they thought that playing with the devil is a good idea. Now you have to clean up the mess, and survive while doing it. Sounds simple on paper, but in practice is not as simple. 

 This game can be pretty challenging especially when you are the only one taking the role of an exorcist. It requires quick reaction time, strategy and knowledge about Azazel's pathing, item spawns, key spawns etc. to have a chance at winning and sending the demon back to hell. Time management is also important, so scavenging items like gas can's or bottles with bleach(?) is a really good idea, but it's not a necessity. You can do a full RNG run and win. Whatever float's your boat.

 Every map has a specific sacrifice that has to be made to complete the ritual. With every burned egg or dumped pig Azazel enters the hunting mode and will try to hunt you down to prevent you from banishing him. And every sacrifice makes them even more aggressive, faster and more resilient to the UV Light - the only "weapon" that you can defend yourself with, so you need to stagger the demon more to calm them down. 

  Time to mention the good and the bad aspects of the game:

  THE GOOD:

- Variety of skin's: It's a small plus and it costs money, but i like the abillity to customise you'r characters look as well as the look of the UV, instead of just generic robes.  BUT...
...youll get certain robes as a gift for completing various "challenges". You can make a collection and they are free so you can still pick something else for your characters without opening your wallet.
- Game is unpredictable: Anything can happen. Of course you have to gather specific items every time you're playing the map, but you will never know when a good run will go to hell in matter of seconds. It's a good mix - you have moment's of peace and repetition just to get slapped in the face later. Also, if you enjoy being chased in horror games you will probably enjoy the thrill of the chase in this game. Especially in the late game, when the ritual is close to being completed.
- The devs don't treat their game too seriously: It may not be a plus to some, but it is a plus for me. You can buy some silly skins and emojis just to goof around a little bit and have some fun. It can be a good way of bonding with others without taking away the fearful aspects of the game. It's a party game after all.
- The creativity of the devs: Every possessed has their own "aesthetics" if i can call it like that, which fit their specific map as well as their background. Sam is a demonic sheriff patrolling abondoned western town called Mercy, Molly is a demonic patient wandering around Mental Facillity and Nathan is a murderous butcher... who looks like he was skinned alive. Different Azazels, different maps with their specific moods. Theres an attention to detail too. 
- Updates and small amount of bugs: Developers are not lazy. They make sure to give us a quality product. However the team is small, so the game itself will be updated less often. 
- It's a full fledged game in general. Feels complete and it's ready to be played.

  THE BAD:

- Scaling the difficulty to Single Player: It's the biggest weakness of this game. Solo runs can be done - not to brag, but i've managed to complete every map on every difficulty, including the Nightmare mode. 
BUT
Since you have to do everything alone, you don't have the same kind of flexibility to explore the whole map without risking something bad happening. Gather items, ritual items, sacrifice, run from Azazel and DON'T DIE. On multi every person can have a specific role and if someone ends up being caught by the possessed they can be revived. The game goes on. On single being caught is a game over. Makes sense, this is the consequence of your failure, however since you don't have a team of 4 people or at least one additional person to help you, this becomes a problem on higher difficulties. 

 RNG in this game matters. Getting an egg that has to be burned upstairs due to the symbol matching the one on the altar in room 8, in the late game with millions of spiders, webs and with angry Zara running around sucks even on Normal mode.  You will most likely drain your UV to kill spiders and get rid of webs and you STILL need to have enough to stun the Spider Lady. If not then you're basically dead, until some miracle happens. On multiplayer you have other people that can protect you or take a hit for you, on solo you have to be constantly on guard, because one, tiny mistake can fuck you over. 

 And NIGHTMARE difficulty is the best example of that.

 In this case game turns from moderately strategic, quick reaction time horror game to luck based Slender The Eight Pages.  It's almost pure RNG. Get unlucky with battery spawn, with minion spawn, Azazel's pathing etc. and its over. You have nothing to defend yourself with unless you found and used a battery to get temporary UV that will give you the abillity to stun the demon once, with good timing. On multiplayer it can be solved by taking simply hits, then reviving downed teammates with medkits and leaving the UV for special situations only. This makes it more manageable but it still goes into unnecessarily hard, luck based range. On solo its just luck, because even the best strat in the world won't save you from enraged Molly running right at you while you were trying to find the darn Duracells.

 Single player needs a few adjustments. Personally, i would nerf the minions: make them spawn later, make less of them or make them slower, especially the ones on The Town. Ghosts are more dangerous than Sam himself, and hes the main antagonist of this map. Its ridiculous. Maybe more batteries on Nightmare for solo plays or the abillity to pick yourself up once during the run. I think that adding an item like a crucifix which will allow you to free yourself from Azazel's grasp once per run for solo players, to give them a second chance would be pretty nice. Those are of course my suggestions. In my opinion devs should think about making some changes to the Single Player mode, without making it "too easy".

 It's a really good and fun game. Despite the big bad that i've mentioned before i still love it as a solo player. I want to see more content in the future and to see it grow. I recommend to buy Devour.

Devour: A Relentless Gauntlet of Jumpscares
Devour is an absolute blast that will put your sanity to the ultimate test. It's one of those horror games that's so terrifying, you'll feel the adrenaline coursing through your veins—I even got so scared I nearly broke my chair on a few occasions. The game is a cooperative horror survival experience where you and your team must perform rituals to banish a demonic entity, and it gets exponentially more difficult the deeper you go.

The game currently features six maps, each with a unique ritual. On the farm, you're tasked with burning goats in a cauldron, while another map requires you to electrocute rats. Each successful ritual ramps up the terror; the main monster becomes faster and more aggressive, eventually entering a deadly hunt mode. To make matters worse, an assortment of horrifying minions, like the crawling cultists and deranged patients, appear more frequently to hinder your progress.

For those looking to customize their experience, there are a variety of cosmetic skins to unlock by playing, along with some truly awesome paid options. The game also supports VR, which is a fantastic idea, though I did notice some performance hiccups that caused a bit of lag during key moments. Despite that, the VR mechanics themselves are very well-done and add an extra layer of immersion to the scares.

Pros
Brutal Jumpscares: This game does not hold back. You are guaranteed to be terrified.

Unique Gameplay per Map: The different rituals on each of the six maps keep the core gameplay fresh and exciting.

Intense Escalation: The difficulty curve is perfectly designed to make you feel overwhelmed and terrified as the ritual progresses.

Cons
VR Performance Issues: The VR mode, while a great addition, could use some optimization to run more smoothly.

Best Played with Friends: The public match community can be sparse, so this game shines brightest when played with a pre-made group.

Final Score
8/10

Devour is an essential pick for any horror fan looking for a co-op experience that will leave them screaming. Just make sure you bring a few friends—and maybe a pillow to hide behind.

Devour is a coop survival horror game that can give you a couple of fun nights with friends, but not much more than that. You play as a group of survivors, and in the first map, The Farmhouse, your goal is to complete a satanic ritual to stop Anna from dragging you to hell. This involves finding goats scattered around the house, feeding them, and sacrificing them at the ritual site. Accessing the goats requires unlocking different rooms throughout the farmhouse, which adds some tension early on. Along the way, demons will randomly spawn and can be killed using your flashlight. Anna herself cannot be killed she can only be stunned briefly with the flashlight, and more often than not, she will catch you. When Anna captures a player, they’re left crawling on the floor similar to PUBG until a teammate revives them with a med kit.The game’s strongest elements are its jump scares and the design of the Farmhouse map. Your first encounter with Anna is especially memorable, and the developers did a solid job creating a sinister, atmospheric environment. For a few hours, the tension works, and the experience is genuinely effective. That said, the game relies heavily on RNG, and careful play or skill alone won’t reliably help you avoid Anna. Over time, the jump scares also lose their impact, and the more you play, the less frightening the game becomes.

I would’ve rated Devour higher if it weren’t for the second map, The Asylum. Here, Anna is replaced by a different boss and goats are swapped out for rats, but the level design takes a noticeable hit. The map feels uninteresting and overly maze-like, to the point where it becomes frustrating rather than tense. My group didn’t even feel motivated to finish it, as it quickly started to feel like a waste of time. I can’t really say Devour is a great game, but it is very cheap, and you’ll likely get around three to four hours of fun out of it if you play with friends. Think of it as a one-night horror party go in with the right expectations, and you might end up enjoying it.

An odd one. Where Phasmophobia is a passive game of baiting the ghost while watching and waiting, Devour is an aggressive game where you have to move move move, and kill kill kill. I really like how proactive the game wants you to be, unlike in Phasmo where a lot of the time it is defensive and just waiting around for the ghost to do something. Devour manages to achieve something which Phasmo hasn't yet. Not to mention character customization and perks. 

Basically, instead of finding ghost evidence and doing bonus objectives, Devour requires you to find and destroy 10 ritual items (goats, rats, eggs, and books) to defeat the monster. The monster is almost always visible and moves around, meaning you can prepare for when it will begin hunting. Hunts are always triggered when you destroy a ritual item, but like in Phasmo they can trigger randomly after a bit. I love how the entire system operates, alongside each ritual item on each map being different in mechanics and destruction.

It has a downside, however. This game is HARD. REALLY hard. In Phasmo, you can clear all maps solo or with just another person with ease, even with minimum gear. In Devour, getting all 10 ritual items as 4 is decently difficult. In the farmhouse map, I played with 2 others, and we would get 8 at most before the monster started hunting every 20-30 seconds and annihilated us. In Phasmo, you can hide and wait out hunts. In Devour, the monster DOESN'T stop hunting until you stun it (more on that later) or if it catches and downs someone. This makes back to back hunts extremely difficult, especially when low on medkits which are required to revive downed teammates. The major difficulty comes in the form of hunts being triggered with every ritual item destroyed, the monster becoming harder to stun with more items destroyed, and the hunts happening back to back like someone binge watching a show. You'll revive your teammate, another teammate will find a ritual item, and then suddenly you hear the monster roar and more likely than not, you will lose a teammate within 20 seconds and have to sack another medkit. 

Now about stunning, stunning is a really stupid mechanic. Unlike in Phasmo, the UV light is a secondary use on your flashlight, and is used for slowing the monster and stunning it, as well as burning minions (more on them later). Remember when I said the monster is harder to stun the more items you destroy? About that...the first stun is almost always easy to nail. If the monster has another charge ready, it becomes IMMUNE to stuns and you're just fucked for a few seconds. Oh, you want to run away while the monster is staggered? The monster did a Dragon Ball fusion with Sonic the Hedgehog. It will run you down HARD. With every item destroyed, it gets faster as well. In my opinion, this game should've either not had stunning required to end a hunt, or at the VERY least just make it only require a single stun, but the monster being slightly longer to stun/gets slowed less by the UV light. There are many places to hide on all of the maps, and you just can't do that to defeat the monster. They feel like filler/leftovers from a different version of the game. "Oh but turning your light off makes you less visible" *sigh* #1 Blinding the player is not a good tradeoff. #2 Is that even true?

Now let's talk about the minions. They are dumb. I love them. I hate them. They are enemies that randomly spawn and mess with you. They require the UV to kill, and you can kill multiple in a single beam which feels amazing. There are 4 types: The crawlers in the Farmhouse, the wheelchairs in the Asylum, the spiders in the Inn, and the Wraiths in the Town. The crawlers and wheelchairs completely immobilize you, and especially with the wheelchairs, sit around corners and surprise freeze you. If you don't UV them quick enough, they'll just kill you right there, especially frustrating during a hunt, as that DOESN'T end the hunt. The spiders and wraiths only slow you, but they slow you down quite a bit. Out of all of them, the spiders and crawlers feel the most fair. The spiders don't freeze you, and the crawlers don't hide around corners. The wraiths fly in the air, are hard to see, and dodge to the side when you're burning them. Absolute hell. Minions overall are better in the game than not, but the amount that spawn in the later stages of games is absurd. You'll destroy some ritual items and all of a sudden, 10 minions are roaming around and you'll just get buttfucked because you have zero UV charge.

Each map has its own gimmick and layout. Farmhouse is highly akin to the Phasmo house maps, with lots of rooms, 2 floors, and all of them being worthwhile to check, with goat burning being the process. Asylum is more like Phasmo Prison than Phasmo Asylum LOL. Big hub area with lots of smaller side areas, with rat electrocution (yes) being the process. Inn is one I love and hate a lot. A beautiful Japanese Inn with lots of sliding door rooms and a creepy cave in the back, with spiders and webs everywhere. Cleansing and offering (?) eggs to altars are the process. Town is the only map in the game I don't like. It's the most unique map aesthetically and layout wise. It's mostly outdoors, with those wraiths roaming and flying everywhere. The monster can even shoot you, infuriatingly when not hunting. Opening lockboxes containing books, empowering (?) them with ritual circles and burning them is the process.

On the subject of opening lockboxes, let's talk about keys. They're not well designed in co-op. Yes, it's realistic that the person that picked the key up is the only one that can use it, but it creates situations where you'll be playing with a bit of a "slower" player who picks up some keys and they don't open important doors until it's too late. This is the case on every map except Asylum, as that map isn't too key crazy. Every other map, however, has keys for tons of rooms, and all of these rooms have only a single entry point. You NEED the key for that room, and to my knowledge the spawns are random for them. If any dev reads this, make keys magically shared with all players. We're playing a game about burning goats, electrocuting rats, washing giant spider eggs before offering them to an altar, empowering books before burning them like we're in WWII Germany, while aiming a UV light at monsters to stun/burn them. We can throw a bit of realism out the door when there's none else to begin with.

All in all, this game is just a great time. Yes, I'm still giving it a positive review, because what's here is incredible. Add more maps, tweak the balance a bit and you'll have something even more marvelous here. Phasmo will fall behind really hard.

Devour is a simple game at its core while also being quite challenging.

The gameplay loop consists of essentially a setup period where you can explore around and move some items around strategically. Once you trigger the first event the game begins and enemies can spawn and the boss will become aggressive. Your goal is to obtain 10 objective items around the level and bring them to the goal. As you progress the game gets more intense with more enemy spawns and a more aggressive/faster boss.

You have limited resources from the start, so if you don't plan ahead you will eventually lose. This includes things like medpacks and flashlight batteries. If the boss reaches a player it will incap them and take them to a random position on the map to be rescued. I'm not sure how this mechanic works if you're playing solo (as I've never done it), but this can get very hectic with a full squad as you try to balance completing the objective and helping others.

All of the maps have their own location and theme, but play similarly to one another. Some of the maps have an added challenge compared to the rest, such as more difficult enemies or a more complex layout. Overall the design of the levels is very good and a large part of the appeal.

There's a bit of an "indie vibe" to the game in that animations are very basic and movement is very simplistic. Having said that, there's a variety of win/defeat cutscenes for each level which is a nice touch.

It's a fun and challenging games with friends, but expect to lose "right at the end" a lot. Perhaps there's an overall strategy that I'm not aware of, but even then there are harder difficulty settings to choose from in that case.

Devour is the perfect mix of panic, teamwork, and “why did I agree to this?” It’s a surprisingly intense co-op horror game where every round feels like a frantic scramble between collecting items and getting jump-scared. The maps are creepy, the progression of the demon keeps the pressure high, and playing with friends is chaotic fun. It’s simple, replayable, and absolutely terrifying in the best way. If you enjoy shouting at your friends while running for your life, this one’s a must-try.
